title: Trigonometric Equations
learningObjective: Find all solutions to a given trigonometric equation.

faqs.question: What's the difference between solving a trig equation "on an interval" versus finding the "general solution"?
faqs.answer: Solving on an interval, like \( [0, 2\pi) \), means listing only the solutions that fall in that one window. The general solution (CheckIt calls this "find all solutions") means describing every solution there is, on the entire number line in both directions, using a formula with an integer \( k \) — because sine, cosine, and tangent repeat forever, the equations studied here repeat their solutions indefinitely, so one solution means infinitely many.

faqs.question: Why does adding 2πk to a solution give another solution?
faqs.answer:
Adding \( 2\pi \) is exactly one full trip around the unit circle, which lands you back on the exact same point — same coordinates, same sine and cosine. So if \( \theta \) is a solution, \( \theta + 2\pi \), \( \theta - 2\pi \), \( \theta + 4\pi \), and so on all share that same point and are solutions too. Writing \( +2\pi k \) for any integer \( k \) captures all of them in one formula. (For the equations studied here, \( 2\pi \) is a period. In other equations, such as \( \sin(\theta/2)=1 \), first find a period that keeps the whole equation true.)

If π/6 solves an equation in sin θ and cos θ (like 2 sin θ − 1 = 0), so do π/6 + 2π, π/6 − 2π, π/6 + 4π, …: they all land on the same point of the unit circle. Writing θ = π/6 + 2πk, for all integers k, captures every one of them at once.

faqs.question: Why do I get ± when I take the square root of a squared trig term?
faqs.answer: This is the same square root property from algebra: if \( x^2 = c \) with \( c \ge 0 \), then \( x = \pm\sqrt{c} \), because a number and its opposite have the same square. It's not optional. In TE3, for squared sine or cosine on \( [0, 2\pi) \), dropping the \( \pm \) usually throws away half of the solutions: the angles for the negative value, which sit in two other quadrants. (When \( c = 1 \), each sign gives one angle, so the count is two. When \( c = 0 \), plus and minus give the same value, so nothing is lost.)

faqs.question: Why might one factor of a factored trig equation have no solution?
faqs.answer:
Sine and cosine can only ever output a number from −1 to 1 — that's their range. If solving one factor requires sine or cosine to equal something outside that range, like 3, there's simply no angle that does that, so that branch contributes nothing to the final answer.

Sine and cosine only ever output values from −1 to 1 (axis broken here to fit "3" on the page). If solving one factor asks for a value outside that range, like cos θ = 3, that factor contributes nothing — it isn't a mistake, just an empty branch.

Extension: factored equations and no-solution branches go beyond the TE3 CheckIt exercise. CheckIt always gives one trig function set equal to a value it can reach.

faqs.question: Why does an equation like sin(2θ) have more solutions on [0, 2π) than sin θ does?
How do I solve a basic trig equation like 2sinθ − 1 = 0 on an interval?
faqs.answer:
Use ordinary algebra to isolate the trig function on one side, just as you would isolate \( x \) in a linear equation. Then use the unit circle or reference angles (TR5) to find every angle in the interval with that value.
Worked Example — solve \( 2\sin\theta - 1 = 0 \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

\( 2\sin\theta = 1 \)  (add 1 to both sides)

\( \sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \)  (divide by 2)

\( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \)  (the two Quadrant I/II angles with sine \( \tfrac{1}{2} \))

faqs.question: How do I write the general solution once I have the interval solutions?
faqs.answer:
Add \( +2\pi k \) (with \( k \) any integer) to each solution you found on \( [0, 2\pi) \). Each interval solution becomes its own family, since coterminal angles repeat every \( 2\pi \). (That works because \( 2\pi \) is a period of the equations in TE3; for other equations, first find a period that keeps the whole equation true.)
Worked Example — general solution of \( 2\sin\theta - 1 = 0 \)

Interval solutions: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \)

General solution: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + 2\pi k \)  and  \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} + 2\pi k, \; k \in \mathbb{Z} \)

faqs.question: How do I solve a trig equation that's already factored into two pieces (Zero Product Property)?
faqs.answer:
Set each factor equal to zero and solve the two simpler equations separately, exactly as you would for a factored polynomial equation. Combine the candidate solutions from both factors into one list, remove duplicates, and reject any angle where the original equation is undefined (for example, where a tangent factor is undefined).
Worked Example — solve \( (2\sin\theta+\sqrt{3})(\cos\theta-1) = 0 \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

\( 2\sin\theta+\sqrt{3}=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3} \)

\( \cos\theta-1=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=0 \)

All solutions: \( \theta = 0, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \)

Extension: factored equations go beyond the TE3 CheckIt exercise.

faqs.question: How do I solve an equation like 4 = 5 + tan θ that involves a different trig function?
faqs.answer:
The algebra step is identical no matter which trig function is involved — isolate it first. What changes is the last step: use the reference angles and quadrant signs for that specific function (tangent's period is π, not 2π, so watch for that when you write the general solution).
Worked Example — solve \( 4 = 5+\tan\theta \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

\( \tan\theta = -1 \)  (subtract 5 from both sides)

\( \theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \)  (tangent is \( -1 \) in Quadrants II and IV)

General solution: \( \theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} + 2\pi k \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{4} + 2\pi k \)

Because \( \tfrac{3\pi}{4} \) and \( \tfrac{7\pi}{4} \) are exactly \( \pi \) apart, \( \theta = \tfrac{3\pi}{4} + \pi k \) is the same set. CheckIt writes the two \( +2\pi k \) lists.

faqs.question: How do I use the square root property on an equation like 4sin²θ − 2 = 0?
faqs.answer:
Isolate the squared trig function first, then take the square root of both sides, keeping both the positive and negative case.
Worked Example — solve \( 4\sin^2\theta - 2 = 0 \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

\( \sin^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \)  (isolate)

\( \sin\theta = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}} = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \)  (square root property, then rationalize — see faq-11)

\( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}, \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \)  (all four quadrants, since both signs are needed)

faqs.question: How do I know which form of a square root value to use (√(1/2) vs √2/2)?
faqs.answer: They're the same number, just written differently — \( \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}} \) rationalizes to \( \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \). Use whichever form you actually recognize on the unit circle (TR5); \( \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \) is the standard form that appears there, so it's usually the more useful one to convert to.

faqs.question: How do I factor out a GCF from a trig equation like 2sinθcosθ − √2cosθ = 0?
faqs.answer:
Look for a factor common to every term — here it's cos θ — pull it out front, and apply the Zero Product Property to the result. Don't divide away a trig factor without separately checking where that factor is zero, since that can quietly delete an entire family of solutions. Factoring is usually safer, because it keeps every solution intact.
Worked Example — solve \( 2\sin\theta\cos\theta - \sqrt{2}\cos\theta = 0 \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

\( \cos\theta(2\sin\theta - \sqrt{2}) = 0 \)  (factor out the GCF, \( \cos\theta \))

\( \cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \)

\( 2\sin\theta-\sqrt{2}=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \)

All solutions: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \)

Extension: factoring out a common factor goes beyond the TE3 CheckIt exercise.

faqs.question: How do I solve a "quadratic in form" trig equation like 2cos²θ − 5cosθ − 3 = 0?
faqs.answer:
Mentally replace the trig function with \( x \), factor the resulting quadratic exactly as in algebra, then switch back and apply the Zero Product Property.
Worked Example — solve \( 2\cos^2\theta - 5\cos\theta - 3 = 0 \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

Let \( x=\cos\theta \): \( 2x^2-5x-3 = (2x+1)(x-3) \)

So \( (2\cos\theta+1)(\cos\theta-3)=0 \)

\( 2\cos\theta+1=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=-\dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\dfrac{4\pi}{3} \)

\( \cos\theta-3=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=3 \) — no solution (faq-14)

Extension: quadratic-form equations go beyond the TE3 CheckIt exercise.

faqs.question: What do I do when a factor from a quadratic-form equation gives no valid solution?
faqs.answer:
Simply drop that branch and report only the solutions from the factor that actually works. This is normal and expected — the algebra of factoring doesn't know sine and cosine are limited to [−1, 1], so it can produce a factor that asks for an impossible value. It isn't a mistake in your work; it's just an empty branch.
Worked Example

From faq-13: \( \cos\theta=3 \) is impossible, so it's discarded.

Final answer: \( \theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \) only.

Extension: CheckIt's TE3 equations always have solutions; empty branches only come up in the factoring extension.

faqs.question: How do I solve an equation with a multiple angle like sin(2θ) = 1/2 for the general solution?
faqs.answer:
Temporarily replace the multiple angle with a single variable, like \( \alpha = 2\theta \), solve for \( \alpha \) as usual (interval solutions, then general solution), and only then substitute \( 2\theta \) back in and solve for \( \theta \) — dividing the whole general solution, period and all, by 2.
Worked Example — general solution of \( \sin(2\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2} \)

Let \( \alpha = 2\theta \): \( \sin\alpha = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{6}+2\pi k \) and \( \alpha = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}+2\pi k \)

Substitute back: \( 2\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}+2\pi k \) and \( 2\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}+2\pi k \)

Divide everything by 2: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{12}+\pi k \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}+\pi k \)

Notice the period is now \( \pi \), not \( 2\pi \) — that's exactly what doubles the count of solutions (faq-5).

Extension: the general solution of a multiple-angle equation goes beyond the TE3 CheckIt exercise, which asks only for the solutions in \( [0, 2\pi) \) (see faq-16).

faqs.question: How do I find all solutions on [0, 2π) once I have the general solution for a multiple-angle equation?
faqs.answer:
Substitute \( k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots \) and then \( k = -1, -2, \ldots \) into each general-solution formula, keeping every result that lands inside \( [0, 2\pi) \). Stop in each direction as soon as a value falls outside the interval.
Worked Example — solutions of \( \sin(2\theta)=\dfrac{1}{2} \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

From \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{12}+\pi k \): \( k=0 \to \dfrac{\pi}{12} \); \( k=1 \to \dfrac{13\pi}{12} \); \( k=2 \to \dfrac{25\pi}{12} \) — too big, stop.

From \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}+\pi k \): \( k=0 \to \dfrac{5\pi}{12} \); \( k=1 \to \dfrac{17\pi}{12} \); \( k=2 \) — too big, stop.

All four solutions: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{12}, \dfrac{5\pi}{12}, \dfrac{13\pi}{12}, \dfrac{17\pi}{12} \)

faqs.question: How does solving these equations use everything from TR5, TE1, and TE2?
faqs.answer:
TR5's reference angles and quadrant signs are how you turn "sin θ = 1/2" into actual angle values, every single time. TE1's identities let you rewrite an equation into a solvable shape, for example replacing sin²θ with 1 − cos²θ (Extension: rewriting with identities goes beyond the TE3 CheckIt exercise; the multiple-angle problems here need only the substitution α = cθ). TE2's habits of manipulating trig expressions — factoring, common denominators, rewriting in sine and cosine — are exactly the algebra skills this section runs on, just now used to solve for θ instead of to prove two sides equal.
Where to start: if the equation looks like this, try this
If the equation looks like…Try…
One trig function, already isolated or easy to isolateIsolate it, then use the unit circle
A squared sine or cosine, like \( \sin^2\theta \)Isolate the square, then take \( \pm \) the square root
A multiple angle, like \( \sin(2\theta) \) or \( \cos(3\theta) \)Let \( \alpha = c\theta \), find every \( \alpha \) in \( [0, 2\pi c) \), divide by \( c \)
Two expressions multiplied, already equal to 0 (Extension)Zero Product Property
A common factor in every term (Extension)Factor out the GCF first; don't divide it away without checking where it is zero
A quadratic if you let \( x = \cos\theta \) or \( \sin\theta \) (Extension)Factor it like \( 2x^2 - 5x - 3 \)

faqs.question: Why does solving trigonometric equations matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Any process that repeats — a wave, a season, a rotating machine part, an alternating current — can often be modeled, exactly or approximately, with sine and cosine (more complicated patterns may need combinations of them), and answering "when does this reach a certain value?" means solving a trig equation. This shows up directly in physics (oscillation and waves), engineering (signal processing, AC circuits), and it's also a skill you'll use in calculus whenever a problem asks where a periodic function crosses zero or hits a maximum. (The applications are beyond the TE3 CheckIt exercise, which asks only for the solutions of given equations.)

guided.title: Which Line Crosses the Circle?
guided.prompt:
I'm practicing TE3 in Math 172: finding where a trig function takes a given value on the unit circle.

What to give me: One equation at a time, written the way CheckIt writes it, with everything on one side, like 2 sin(theta) - sqrt(3) = 0 or 3 sec(theta) + 2 sqrt(3) = 0. Use all six trig functions over the session.

Allowed values: Only values the function actually takes at a unit-circle angle:
- sin or cos: 0, plus or minus 1/2, plus or minus sqrt(2)/2, plus or minus sqrt(3)/2, or plus or minus 1
- tan or cot: 0, plus or minus sqrt(3)/3, plus or minus 1, or plus or minus sqrt(3)
- sec or csc: plus or minus 1, plus or minus 2 sqrt(3)/3, plus or minus sqrt(2), or plus or minus 2

Must include: At least one problem where the value is 1 or -1 for sin, cos, sec, or csc.

What I'll do before listing any angles:
1. Isolate the function.
2. If it is sec, csc, or cot, flip it to cos, sin, or tan and simplify. (If you give cot(theta) = 0, I'll rewrite cot as cos over sin instead of flipping.)
3. Say which line I'd draw on the unit circle: horizontal for sine, vertical for cosine, a line through the origin for tangent.
4. Predict how many angles in [0, 2pi) I'll get.

Ask me to justify each step before you confirm it. Then I'll list the angles in [0, 2pi).

Your planted mistake: On the fourth problem, show me your own solution with one deliberate mistake (for example, forgetting to flip a reciprocal function, or picking the wrong quadrants for a negative value) and ask me to find it.

After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Grade a Classmate's "All Solutions" Answers
guided.prompt:
I'm practicing "find all solutions" problems for TE3 in Math 172. CheckIt writes the answer as a list of angles, each with + 2 pi k, followed by "for all integers k", for example: theta = pi/6 + 2 pi k, 5 pi/6 + 2 pi k for all integers k.

What to show me: One equation at a time, together with an answer a classmate wrote.
- The equation is in CheckIt's form: sin, cos, tan, csc, sec, or cot equal to a value that function takes at a unit-circle angle, with everything on one side.
- Some classmate answers should be correct. Some should be missing a family. Some should use + pi k for sine or cosine.
- At least one should be a tangent or cotangent answer written as a single family with + pi k that is actually correct.
- At least one should be a sine or cosine answer that is correctly written with + pi k, like sin(theta) = 0 giving theta = pi k, so I see that + pi k is not only for tangent and cotangent.

What I'll do: Decide whether the answer is right. If it isn't, I'll explain what is wrong and write the corrected answer in CheckIt's form. Don't tell me whether I'm right until I've explained my reasoning.

Your planted mistake: On the fourth problem, grade the classmate's answer yourself, with one deliberate mistake in your grading, and ask me to find it.

After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Factor Before You Solve
guided.prompt:
This is an extension beyond the TE3 CheckIt exercise. I'm practicing trig equations that need factoring before I can use the unit circle.

What to give me: One equation at a time, to solve on [0, 2pi). Use three kinds:
- already factored, like (2 sin(theta) + 1)(cos(theta) - 1) = 0
- with a common factor, like 2 sin(theta) cos(theta) - cos(theta) = 0
- quadratic in form, like 2 cos^2(theta) - cos(theta) - 1 = 0

Values: Every factor should set sin, cos, or tan equal to a unit-circle value. The exception: one problem should include a factor that asks for a value sine or cosine can never reach, like cos(theta) = 2.

What I'll do: Before I factor, I'll say which kind of factoring the equation needs. After I factor, I'll solve each factor separately, combine the lists, remove duplicates, and reject any angle where the original equation is undefined (for example, where tan(theta) is undefined). Ask me questions instead of doing the steps for me.

Your planted mistake: On the third problem, show me your own solution with one deliberate mistake (for example, dividing both sides by cos(theta) instead of factoring it out, or dropping a factor that gives only one angle) and ask me to find it.

After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Predict the Count: Squared Equations
guided.prompt:
I'm practicing squared trig equations for TE3 in Math 172.

What to give me: One equation at a time, written the way CheckIt writes it, like 4 sin^2(theta) - 3 = 0, and ask for all solutions in the interval [0, 2pi).

Allowed values: Only sin^2(theta) or cos^2(theta), and only 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, or 1 for the square, so every answer is a unit-circle angle.

Must include: At least one problem where the square equals 1 and one where it equals 0.

What I'll do:
1. Isolate the square.
2. Take the square root with plus or minus, and simplify (rationalize if needed).
3. Predict how many angles I'll get before I list them.

Ask me to explain my prediction with horizontal lines (for sine) or vertical lines (for cosine) on the unit circle. Remind me that 0 is in [0, 2pi) and 2pi is not.

Your planted mistake: On the fourth problem, show me your own solution with one deliberate mistake (for example, dropping the minus sign, or listing 2pi as an answer; if you drop the minus sign, use a problem where the square is not 0, so the mistake actually changes the answer) and ask me to find it.

After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Count the Laps: Multiple-Angle Equations
guided.prompt:
I'm practicing multiple-angle equations for TE3 in Math 172, like 2 cos(3 theta) + 1 = 0, where I find all solutions in the interval [0, 2pi).

What to give me: One equation at a time, written the way CheckIt writes it, using only sin(c theta) or cos(c theta) with c = 2, 3, or 4.

Allowed values: 0, plus or minus 1/2, plus or minus sqrt(2)/2, plus or minus sqrt(3)/2, or plus or minus 1.

Must include: Each of c = 2, 3, and 4 at least once, and one problem where the value is 1 or -1.

What I'll do:
1. Isolate the trig function.
2. Let alpha = c theta and say how far alpha runs: from 0 up to, but not including, 2 pi times c.
3. List every alpha in that range, lap by lap.
4. Divide each by c.
5. Check that my count makes sense and that every answer is in [0, 2pi).

Ask me questions instead of doing the steps for me.

Your planted mistake: On the third problem, show me your own solution with one deliberate mistake (for example, stopping after one lap, or keeping an angle that is 2pi or more after dividing) and ask me to find it.

After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

open.title: Create Your Own
open.prompt: Use the AI tool of your choice. Start by describing what you're confused about or curious about from Section TE3 (Trigonometric Equations). Ask the AI to help you explore that idea one question at a time, without solving your CheckIt problem for you. Before you trust any answer it gives, check one claim it makes against your notes or the TE3 support page. For example, check whether an angle it gives really has the right sine or cosine, or whether an answer it lists is actually in [0, 2pi). Share what you learned, what surprised you, and anything the AI got wrong.

paths.label: TE3: Trigonometric Equations
paths.intro: Builds to the TE3 check: find all solutions of a basic trig equation, and the solutions in [0, 2π) of a squared equation and a multiple-angle equation. Practice scope: the path practises all three TE3 CheckIt problems in CheckIt's forms: any of the six functions (answers written with +2πk for all integers k), sin² or cos² equations (including values that give only two angles), and sin(cθ) or cos(cθ) with c = 2, 3 or 4. The stop "Extension: Factoring quadratic-form equations" goes beyond the TE3 CheckIt exercise and is optional.

stages.desc: Three quick reviews TE3 leans on: the unit circle in reverse (TR5), tangent and reciprocal functions, and the algebra of isolating and square roots. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Unit circle in reverse
stops.target: Given a sine or cosine value, find every angle in \([0,2\pi)\) with that value (TR5). Sine is the \(y\)-coordinate (draw a horizontal line); cosine is the \(x\)-coordinate (draw a vertical line).
stops.coldPlain: Find all theta in [0, 2pi): (1) cos theta = -1/2 (2) sin theta = sqrt2/2
stops.solution: (1) Reference angle pi/3; cosine is negative in Quadrants II and III: 2pi/3 and 4pi/3. (2) Reference angle pi/4; sine is positive in Quadrants I and II: pi/4 and 3pi/4.
stops.mistake: Stopping at one angle; most values appear twice in [0, 2pi).
stops.reflect: Why does a horizontal line usually hit the unit circle twice?

stops.title: Tangent and the reciprocal functions
stops.target: Find angles for \(\tan\theta\), and turn \(\csc\), \(\sec\), \(\cot\) equations into \(\sin\), \(\cos\), \(\tan\) by flipping.
stops.coldPlain: Find all theta in [0, 2pi): (1) tan theta = -sqrt3 (2) csc theta = -2sqrt3/3
stops.solution: (1) Tangent is negative in Quadrants II and IV, and tan(pi/3) = sqrt3, so the reference angle is pi/3: 2pi/3 and 5pi/3. (2) Flip: sin theta = -3/(2sqrt3) = -sqrt3/2. Reference angle pi/3; sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV: 4pi/3 and 5pi/3.
stops.mistake: Treating csc theta = -2sqrt3/3 as sin theta = -2sqrt3/3 (about -1.15, so "no solution") instead of flipping to -sqrt3/2.
stops.reflect: Why are tangent solutions always exactly pi apart?

stops.title: Algebra: isolate, square roots, rationalize
stops.target: Solve linear and squared equations for \(x\), keep both signs of a square root, and rationalize (for example, \(1/\sqrt{2}=\sqrt{2}/2\)).
stops.solution: (1) 2x = -sqrt3, x = -sqrt3/2. (2) x^2 = 6/8 = 3/4, x = plus or minus sqrt3/2. (3) x^2 = 2/4 = 1/2, x = plus or minus 1/sqrt2 = plus or minus sqrt2/2.
stops.mistake: Writing only the positive square root.
stops.reflect: Every TE3 CheckIt equation turns into one of these once you put a trig function (or c theta inside one) in place of x. Which algebra step is slowest for you?

stages.desc: Isolate and solve on [0, 2π), all solutions with 2πk, reciprocal functions, squared functions, and multiple angles. The last stop, factoring, is an optional extension.

stops.title: Isolate, then use the unit circle
stops.target: Solve on \([0,2\pi)\): isolate the trig function with algebra, find the reference angle, then pick the quadrants from the sign. (If the value is 0, 1, or −1, the angles are on the axes: read them straight off the unit circle.)
stops.cold: Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(2\sin\theta+\sqrt2=0\).
stops.coldPlain: Find all solutions in the interval [0, 2pi) of 2 sin theta + sqrt2 = 0.
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: sin theta = -sqrt2/2. Reference angle pi/4. Sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV: 5pi/4 and 7pi/4.
stops.mistake: Answering -pi/4, which is not in [0, 2pi); its coterminal angle 7pi/4 is.
stops.again: Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(2\cos\theta+\sqrt3=0\).
stops.reflect: How does the sign of the value tell you which quadrants to use?

stops.title: All solutions: add 2πk
stops.target: "Find all solutions" means every angle, not just \([0,2\pi)\). Find the solutions in \([0,2\pi)\), then add \(2\pi k\) to each.
stops.coldPlain: Find all solutions of 2 sin theta + sqrt3 = 0.
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: sin theta = -sqrt3/2. Reference angle pi/3; sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV, so 4pi/3 and 5pi/3 in [0, 2pi). Sine repeats every 2pi, so all solutions are 4pi/3 + 2pi k and 5pi/3 + 2pi k for every integer k.
stops.mistake: Writing only 4pi/3 + 2pi k and losing the second family, or writing 4pi/3 + pi k (that list includes pi/3, where sine is positive).
stops.againA: \(\tan\theta=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\): \(\theta=\tfrac{5\pi}{6}+2\pi k,\ \tfrac{11\pi}{6}+2\pi k\) (the same angles as \(\tfrac{5\pi}{6}+\pi k\)).
stops.reflect: Look at the graph: what does k count?

stops.title: Equations with csc, sec, or cot
stops.target: Isolate the reciprocal function, flip to sine, cosine, or tangent, and simplify the value before you use the unit circle. (cot θ = 0 can\'t be flipped: it means cos θ = 0.)
stops.coldPlain: Find all solutions of 3 csc theta - 2 sqrt3 = 0.
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: csc theta = 2sqrt3/3. Flip: sin theta = 3/(2sqrt3) = sqrt3/2. That gives pi/3 and 2pi/3, so pi/3 + 2pi k and 2pi/3 + 2pi k.
stops.mistake: Flipping 2sqrt3/3 to 3/(2sqrt3) and not recognizing it as sqrt3/2 (multiply top and bottom by sqrt3).
stops.stretchA: You can't flip 0. Instead, \(\cot\theta=\tfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=0\) exactly when \(\cos\theta=0\) (and \(\sin\theta\ne0\) there): \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{2}+2\pi k,\ \tfrac{3\pi}{2}+2\pi k\).
stops.reflect: Why is it safer to flip to sin, cos, or tan than to memorize csc, sec, cot values?

stops.title: Squared trig functions: ± usually doubles the count
stops.target: Isolate \(\sin^2\theta\) or \(\cos^2\theta\), take both square roots, and solve each sign separately.
stops.cold: Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(4\cos^2\theta-1=0\).
stops.coldPlain: Find all solutions in the interval [0, 2pi) of 4 cos^2 theta - 1 = 0.
stops.note: Show the isolated square, both signs of the square root, and the angles for each sign.
stops.solution: cos^2 theta = 1/4, so cos theta = plus or minus 1/2. Positive: pi/3, 5pi/3. Negative: 2pi/3, 4pi/3. Four solutions.
stops.mistake: Taking only cos theta = 1/2 and stopping at two answers.
stops.again: Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(\sin^2\theta-1=0\).
stops.againA: \(\sin\theta=\pm1\): \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\). The lines \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\) each touch the circle at only one point, so the count is two, not four.
stops.stretch: Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(\sin^2\theta=0\). Why doesn't the \(\pm\) add any angles?
stops.stretchA: \(\sin\theta=\pm0=0\): \(\theta=0,\ \pi\). Plus 0 and minus 0 are the same number, so there is only one line, \(y=0\). And 0 counts, because it is in \([0,2\pi)\).
stops.reflect: Look at the picture: how do the two vertical lines explain why there are four answers?

stops.title: Multiple angles: sin(3θ), cos(2θ)
stops.target: For \(\sin(c\theta)\) or \(\cos(c\theta)\) on \([0,2\pi)\), let \(\alpha=c\theta\). Then \(\alpha\) runs over \([0,2\pi c)\): find every \(\alpha\) there, lap by lap, then divide each by \(c\).
stops.cold: Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(2\sin(3\theta)-1=0\).
stops.coldPlain: Find all solutions in the interval [0, 2pi) of 2 sin(3 theta) - 1 = 0.
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, how far alpha = c theta runs, every alpha lap by lap, and the division by c.
stops.solution: sin(3 theta) = 1/2. Let alpha = 3 theta; alpha goes from 0 to 6pi (three trips around the circle). alpha = pi/6, 5pi/6, 13pi/6, 17pi/6, 25pi/6, 29pi/6. Divide by 3: pi/18, 5pi/18, 13pi/18, 17pi/18, 25pi/18, 29pi/18.
stops.mistake: Solving sin alpha = 1/2 only in [0, 2pi), dividing by 3, and reporting just pi/18 and 5pi/18.
stops.again: Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(2\cos(2\theta)+1=0\).
stops.reflect: Before solving, how can you predict how many answers sin(c theta) = (a value) will have on [0, 2pi)? When is the count smaller?

stops.title: Extension: Factoring quadratic-form equations (beyond the TE3 CheckIt exercise)
stops.target: Treat the trig function like a variable, factor, set each factor to zero, and drop any factor that asks for an impossible value.
stops.cold: Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(2\sin^2\theta-\sin\theta-1=0\).
stops.coldPlain: Find all solutions in the interval [0, 2pi) of 2 sin^2 theta - sin theta - 1 = 0.
stops.note: Show the factored form, each factor set to zero, and any factor that gives no angle.
stops.solution: Let u = sin theta: 2u^2 - u - 1 = (2u + 1)(u - 1). sin theta = -1/2 gives 7pi/6 and 11pi/6; sin theta = 1 gives pi/2.
stops.mistake: Dropping the factor sin theta - 1 = 0 because it gives only one angle, or forgetting to switch back from u to sin theta. (In the stretch, never divide both sides by cos theta: you would lose pi/2 and 3pi/2.)
stops.again: Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1=0\).
stops.stretch: Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta-\sqrt2\cos\theta=0\).
stops.reflect: What would you do if one factor gave cos theta = 3?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the TE3 CheckIt: three equations.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Find all solutions of a basic trig equation, and solutions in [0, 2pi) of a squared and a multiple-angle equation.
stops.cold:
(1) Find all solutions of the equation \(\sec\theta-2=0\).
(2) Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of the equation \(\cos^2\theta=0\).
(3) Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of the equation \(2\cos(3\theta)+1=0\).
stops.coldPlain: (1) Find all solutions of sec theta - 2 = 0. (2) Find all solutions in [0, 2pi) of cos^2 theta = 0. (3) Find all solutions in [0, 2pi) of 2 cos(3 theta) + 1 = 0.
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: (1) sec theta = 2, so cos theta = 1/2: pi/3 and 5pi/3 in [0, 2pi), so pi/3 + 2pi k and 5pi/3 + 2pi k. (2) cos theta = plus or minus 0 = 0: pi/2 and 3pi/2. (3) cos(3 theta) = -1/2; alpha = 3 theta in [0, 6pi): 2pi/3, 4pi/3, 8pi/3, 10pi/3, 14pi/3, 16pi/3; divide by 3.
stops.mistake: In (3), dividing 2pi/3 by 3 but forgetting the other trips around the circle.
stops.again: (1) Find all solutions of the equation \(\csc\theta+1=0\). (2) Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(4\cos^2\theta-1=0\). (3) Find all solutions in the interval \([0,2\pi)\) of \(\sin(4\theta)-1=0\).
stops.againA: (1) \(\sin\theta=-1\): \(\theta=\tfrac{3\pi}{2}+2\pi k\) for all integers \(k\) (one angle per lap, so one family). (2) \(\cos\theta=\pm\tfrac12\): \(\tfrac{\pi}{3},\tfrac{2\pi}{3},\tfrac{4\pi}{3},\tfrac{5\pi}{3}\). (3) \(\alpha=4\theta\in[0,8\pi)\): \(\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{5\pi}{2},\tfrac{9\pi}{2},\tfrac{13\pi}{2}\), so \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{8},\tfrac{5\pi}{8},\tfrac{9\pi}{8},\tfrac{13\pi}{8}\).
stops.reflect: Which question type is trickiest: all solutions, squared, or multiple angle?
